```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

This vignette shows how to classify European vegetation relevés into **EUNIS habitat types** using the expert system of Chytrý et al. ([2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12519)). Habitat descriptions are available on [FloraVeg.EU](https://floraveg.eu/habitat/) (Chytrý et al. [2024](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12798)) and the [EEA EUNIS website](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/datahub/datahubitem-view/123d0c9a-a6fa-4f2d-b887-5d8e5468faed).

First, `resy_harmonize_eunis()` prepares the plot data. It adds geographic information such as country, ecoregion and coastal position, and checks and adjusts the coordinate format and species names to meet the expert system's requirements. Then, `resy_classify()` assigns the relevés to habitat types using their species composition and site data.

## Example

The following R packages are required to run the example of this vignette:

```{r libraries, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
library(RESY)
```

### Load the example data

The example data include the species table with the vegetation relevés and the header table with the location of each relevé.

First, load the vegetation relevés:

```{r example-data-species, message=FALSE}
data_species <- read_csv(
  system.file("extdata", "data_example_species.csv", package = "RESY")
  )
data_species
```

`resy_clean_names()` removes the author names from the species names and keeps
rank markers such as `subsp.` and `var.`:

```{r clean-species-names, message=FALSE}
data_species$scientificName <- resy_clean_names(
  data_species$scientificName
  )
```

Second, load the header table:

```{r example-data-sites, message=FALSE}
data_sites <- read_csv(
   system.file("extdata", "data_example_sites.csv", package = "RESY")
   ) |>
   st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326)
data_sites
```

### Map the sites

The vegetation relevés of the example dataset are in Tuscany in Italy.

```{r base-map, echo=FALSE}
utils::data(
  "europe_resolution_1_epsg25832", package = "RESY", envir = environment()
  )
bbox <- data_sites |>
   st_transform(crs = 25832) |>
   st_bbox()
ggplot() +
   geom_sf(data = europe_resolution_1_epsg25832) +
   geom_sf(
      data = data_sites |> st_transform(crs = 25832),
      colour = "black", size = 1
      ) +
   annotate(
      geom = "text", x = 660000, y = 4800000, label = "Italy-Tuscany"
      ) +
   coord_sf(
      xlim = bbox[c("xmin", "xmax")],
      ylim = bbox[c("ymin", "ymax")],
      expand = TRUE
   ) +
   theme_classic()
```

The map shows part of Italy, mainly Tuscany, and the Tyrrhenian Sea. The dots are the locations of the vegetation relevés. Some are on islands.

## Get additional data

### Load the expert system

`resy_load_expert()` reads the EUNIS expert system. `resy_harmonize_eunis()` uses it to check the species names.

```{r parse-expert-file}
parsed_expert_file <- resy_load_expert(scheme = "EUNIS")
```

### Apply `resy_harmonize_eunis()`

`resy_harmonize_eunis()` prepares the header table and the species table:

```{r use-check-eunis}
outcome <- resy_harmonize_eunis(
   data = data_sites,
   run_taxonomy = TRUE,
   species_data = data_species,
   parsed = parsed_expert_file,
   run_coast_dunes = TRUE,
   coast_buffer = 5000
   )
```

`resy_harmonize_eunis()` gives two warnings. The first says that the column `Altitude (m)` is missing: `resy_harmonize_eunis()` cannot add it, but `vignette("altitude-vignette")` shows how to get it. The second says that the ecoregion column (`Ecoreg`) contains `NA` values for sites outside the ecoregion base map.

### Inspect additional data

Here is the header table with the ecoregions and countries that `resy_harmonize_eunis()` added:

```{r show-added-ecoregions}
outcome$sites
```

### Missing info

These vegetation relevés did not get an ecoregion:

```{r missing-info}
outcome$sites |>
   filter(is.na(Ecoreg))
```

All 23 of these plots are on the Mediterranean coast (`Coast_EEA` is `MED_COAST`), where the ecoregion base map does not reach. Their country was found. In your own data, set their ecoregion before classifying. This example leaves them unset, so `resy_classify()` evaluates their ecoregion as 0 and warns.

Here is the updated map with the ecoregions in different colors:

```{r map-2, echo=FALSE}
ggplot() +
   geom_sf(data = europe_resolution_1_epsg25832) +
   geom_sf(
      data = outcome$sites |>
         st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326),
      aes(color = as.factor(Ecoreg))
      ) +
   annotate(
      geom = "text", x = 660000, y = 4800000, label = "Italy-Tuscany"
      ) +
   coord_sf(
      xlim = bbox[c("xmin", "xmax")],
      ylim = bbox[c("ymin", "ymax")],
      expand = TRUE
   ) +
   theme_classic()
```

### Checked species names

`outcome$species_checked` has one row per species name: the name in the data (`scientificName`), the name the expert system uses (`TaxonName`) and whether it matched (`matched`):

```{r checked-species-names}
outcome$species_checked
```

```{r summary-checked-species-names}
summary(outcome$species_checked)
```

### Finalize species data

`resy_classify()` needs the checked names together with the cover of each species, so the species table is joined to the checked names:

```{r prepare-outcome_species2}
outcome_species <- data_species |>
  left_join(outcome$species_checked, by = "scientificName") |>
  select(PlotObservationID, TaxonName, Cover_Perc)
outcome_species |>
  filter(PlotObservationID == "AE28") |>
  arrange(desc(Cover_Perc), TaxonName)
```

## Classify relevés

`resy_classify()` classifies the vegetation relevés (`obs`) using the site data in the header table (`header`):

```{r apply-resy-classify}
res <- resy_classify(
  obs = outcome_species,
  header = outcome$sites,
  scheme = "EUNIS"
  )
```

`resy_classify()` warns about the site data that is missing: the header has no
`Altitude (m)` and no `Dataset` column (one EUNIS rule excludes the Swedish
National Forest Inventory), and 23 plots have no ecoregion.

## Inspect results

### Long table of candidates for all plots

Plot AM30 meets the rules of two EUNIS habitat types, T17 and its parent T. It
is assigned to T17, which has the higher priority.

```{r show-eunis-candidates-long}
cand <- resy_candidates(res, top_n = 3)
cand
```

`wide = TRUE` gives one row per plot: the type it is classified as, then its
candidate types with their priorities, highest priority first:

```{r show-eunis-candidates-wide}
resy_candidates(res, top_n = 3, wide = TRUE)
```

### Plot-level details

`resy_eval_plot()` prints the full evidence for one plot: its species, which
vegetation-type formulas evaluated to `TRUE`, and the type it is classified as.
It then lists the lower-level types the plot did not reach, with the result of
each of their conditions, which shows why the classification stopped at this
level.

```{r eval-plot}
resy_eval_plot(res, p = "AM30") # p = PlotObservationID
```

Passing `type` explains any other type in the same way, whether or not its
rule holds for the plot:

```{r eval-plot-type}
resy_eval_plot(res, p = "AM30", type = "T17")
```

### Print classification hierarchy

`resy_expert_tree()` prints the type hierarchy of an expert system. In this
example, it is the
[EUNIS](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/datahub/datahubitem-view/123d0c9a-a6fa-4f2d-b887-5d8e5468faed)
expert system, and the tree lists all its types, whether or not they occur in
your data. `fill = TRUE` adds the group levels that the type codes imply but the
expert system does not list, here `MA2` and `MA22`. The output is cut to the
first 10 types. Descriptions of all EUNIS habitat types are on
[FloraVeg.EU](https://floraveg.eu/habitat/).

```{r print-results-of-classification}
resy_expert_tree(parsed_expert_file, fill = TRUE) |>
  head(10)
```
